allowed_claims: Simple Analytics requires no cookies, no trackers, and no consent from visitors.

The Self-serve plan includes 1 user; each additional user costs +€20/month.

Website data is stored in the EU, with primary infrastructure in the Netherlands.
Data only goes to a provider outside the EU when the customer opts in to a feature that needs it, such as the AI assistant.
By default, Simple Analytics does not collect or store any data for visitors who have Do Not Track enabled.
Simple Analytics collects and stores how long a page is viewed, counting seconds only while the page is visible and not when it is hidden.
Simple Analytics collects and stores how far a visitor scrolls on a page, recorded in 5% increments.
All analytics data is processed in the Netherlands (EU-hosted).
No IP addresses are stored; they are discarded immediately.
Data is encrypted, and only Simple Analytics controls the decryption keys.
Simple Analytics is hosted on infrastructure from Worldstream and Leaseweb.
Simple Analytics does not process personal data, so a Data Processing Agreement is not required when using it.
Simple Analytics processes only Page URL, Referrer, UTM parameters, Time zone, and Device and browser type as its data scope.
The installation flow is technology-dependent: Simple Analytics scans each site and offers install code based on detected technologies rather than a single universal step.
Across Simple Analytics generally, additional websites/subdomains added to an account do not cost extra individually, but are capped by a plan-wide website limit.

assets.title: Analytics without cookies or trackers
assets.content:
Subject: Analytics without cookies or trackers
Preview text: Evaluate a clear privacy model for client-site analytics.

Evaluate analytics without cookies or trackers

Hi there,

When consent and personal-data handling affect a client-site decision, you can evaluate analytics with a specific operating model: no cookies, no trackers and no visitor consent required for Simple Analytics itself.

Simple Analytics is privacy-friendly website analytics designed to measure traffic without processing personal data. Under GDPR, that absence of personal-data processing means a DPA is not required when using Simple Analytics.

That gives you concrete privacy mechanics to assess for each client site, rather than a broad “privacy-friendly” label. You can decide whether the model fits the site and the recommendation you need to make.

The signup page opens a 14-day self-serve trial, so you can explore Simple Analytics on your own.

Start your 14-day trial → https://www.simpleanalytics.com/signup

- Simple Analytics

asset_metadata.single_idea: If consent and personal-data processing affect what you can recommend to clients, Simple Analytics is worth considering because it operates without cookies or trackers, requires no visitor consent for its analytics and states that it does not process personal data.

selected_brief.selection_reason: Consent and personal-data handling are documented decision criteria for this audience, and Simple Analytics has direct evidence for the mechanism rather than relying on the vague label “privacy-friendly.”

value_case.reader_benefit: For client sites where consent and DPA requirements shape the analytics choice, the developer can consider an analytics option designed to provide website measurement without processing personal data or requiring visitor consent for Simple Analytics itself.
value_case.mechanism: Simple Analytics uses no cookies or trackers and states that visitor consent is not required. It also states that it does not process personal data, which is why a DPA is not required under the documented GDPR basis.
decision_conditions: Apply the claim to Simple Analytics' documented data practices, not as universal legal advice for every client configuration or jurisdiction.
Each client website still requires its own appropriate installation and fit assessment.

claim_conditions: The no-consent claim concerns Simple Analytics' own documented operation.
The DPA statement is based on Simple Analytics not processing personal data and should not be generalized to every vendor, client configuration or jurisdiction.
Add each website and use the technology-detected HTML code or another documented platform or framework installation option.

The documented per-site installation and privacy behavior support an exploratory product evaluation across client builds, but R15 describes the additional-website rule in a subdomain context and does not establish the Self-serve site cap or aggregate portfolio cost; the research also does not verify firsthand agency demand or recipient qualification.
These sources document Simple Analytics' own behavior and stated GDPR basis; they do not establish a universal legal conclusion for every client configuration or jurisdiction.
selected_brief.target_audience: Agency or freelance developer choosing the analytics stack for client sites
selected_brief.job: Earn a self-guided evaluation by giving the reader a concrete, documented reason to consider Simple Analytics for client work where consent and personal-data handling matter.
selected_brief.single_idea: If consent and personal-data processing affect what you can recommend to clients, Simple Analytics is worth considering because it operates without cookies or trackers, requires no visitor consent for its analytics and states that it does not process personal data.
selected_brief.felt_need: Whether adopting a cookie-free or 'privacy-friendly' analytics tool actually removes the need for a cookie consent banner is directly disputed among developers, with claims that named alternatives (Fathom, Plausible) still use techniques that may require consent, and skepticism that first-party analytics cookies qualify as 'strictly necessary.'
selected_brief.mechanism: Anchor the pitch in the documented operating model: no cookies, no trackers and no visitor consent required; no personal-data processing, which is the stated basis for not requiring a DPA. Then offer the documented 14-day self-guided trial rather than asking the reader to accept the positioning on faith.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: For a reader actively evaluating analytics alongside GA4, an assisted comparison is a distinct reason to engage: it defines a measurement question and reviews methodological causes over a fixed 30-day run.

value_case.reader_benefit: A developer or agency with an active GA4 comparison can evaluate reported pageview trends on a real site while receiving help interpreting differences instead of treating the raw gap as a consent-rejection figure.
value_case.mechanism: The assisted proof of concept begins by defining the measurement question, then runs Simple Analytics alongside GA4 for 30 days and reviews weekly trends against factors including duplicate tags, SPA routing, bot filtering, consent configuration and reporting identity.
decision_conditions: Relevant only when the reader has an active GA4 comparison to run.
The proof of concept requires booking a demo and keeping GA4 and the existing consent banner in place during the comparison.

claim_conditions: The comparison does not isolate or quantify a consent-rejection rate from the raw pageview difference.
The offer is an assisted enterprise-oriented proof of concept, not the self-serve trial.
Add each website and use the technology-detected HTML code or another documented platform or framework installation option.

The documented per-site installation and privacy behavior support an exploratory product evaluation across client builds, but R15 describes the additional-website rule in a subdomain context and does not establish the Self-serve site cap or aggregate portfolio cost; the research also does not verify firsthand agency demand or recipient qualification.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: If you need to compare Simple Analytics with GA4 on a real site, the free 30-day assisted proof of concept provides a defined measurement question and a weekly review of the methodological causes behind differing pageview trends.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Define the measurement question with Simple Analytics, run both systems alongside the existing consent setup for 30 days, and review weekly pageview trends against documented methodological causes.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: a side-by-side analytics comparison is just two totals with an ambiguous gap. After: the reader sees a structured, assisted way to examine the methodological factors behind that gap on their own site.
must_not_say: Do not assume the recipient currently uses GA4; make the proposition conditional.
Do not describe the pageview gap as a consent-rejection rate or promise to isolate a consent-specific figure.
Do not claim the proof of concept guarantees higher counts, accuracy, revenue gains or a migration decision.
Do not present the assisted proof of concept as part of the self-serve trial.
alternative_arguments.objection: A raw comparison could produce different totals without explaining what caused the difference.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Book a demo to define what you would compare in the free 30-day proof of concept.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether an assisted 30-day comparison alongside GA4 is appropriate for the site's measurement question.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The demo begins the process of discussing the GA4 setup, defining the measurement question and agreeing what the 30-day comparison should examine.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Booking the demo does not establish the eventual size or cause of any pageview difference and does not produce a consent-rejection rate.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Signal a concrete 30-day side-by-side evaluation, while making clear that the purpose is to understand the numbers rather than promise a predetermined gap.

selected_brief.belief_shift: Before: “privacy-friendly” is an ambiguous category claim. After: Simple Analytics has a specific operating model the reader can evaluate—no cookies, no trackers, no required visitor consent and no personal-data processing.
must_not_say: Do not claim that every client site or jurisdiction can remove its entire consent banner solely by installing Simple Analytics.
Do not claim universal legal compliance or give legal advice.
Do not claim other privacy-friendly analytics products use fingerprinting, require consent or process personal data.
Do not assume the recipient currently uses GA4, has experienced a compliance failure or manages a particular number of sites.
Do not claim one plan covers arbitrary client domains at a known aggregate price or omit the existence of plan-wide website limits.
Do not promise faster implementation, time savings, revenue gains, higher data accuracy or a quantified increase in pageviews.
Do not introduce the full security, hosting, scroll-depth, time-on-page, AI-assistant or competitor-comparison catalogue.
Do not describe the 14-day self-serve trial as including the assisted 30-day GA4 comparison.
selected_brief.objection: Privacy-friendly analytics claims can be hard to distinguish when the consent and personal-data mechanics are not explicit.
selected_brief.tone: Matter-of-fact, concise and reassuring; explain the cause and consequence without urgency or hype.
selected_brief.next_step_decision: Decide whether Simple Analytics' documented privacy model and product experience are suitable for a client-site analytics evaluation.
selected_brief.next_step_value: The signup path provides a 14-day self-serve trial in which the reader can explore Simple Analytics on their own.
selected_brief.next_step_limit: The self-guided trial does not include the assisted 30-day comparison alongside GA4 and does not establish legal suitability across every client configuration or jurisdiction.
selected_brief.subject_strategy: Lead with the concrete operating distinction—analytics without cookies, trackers or personal-data processing—rather than a generic privacy claim or fear-based compliance language.

reader_verdicts.what_it_sells: A self-serve website analytics tool for client sites that claims to measure traffic without cookies, trackers, or personal-data processing, potentially reducing consent-banner and DPA work.
reader_verdicts.relevance_feedback: The profile explicitly establishes that I choose analytics stacks for client sites, so evaluating privacy mechanics is relevant. The email appropriately conditions its premise with “When consent and personal-data handling affect a client-site decision” rather than claiming this is currently blocking me. Whether I need a repeatable default, face consent or DPA friction now, or would consider a paid alternative remains unknown.
assumed_experiences: Profile-supported: I choose analytics technology for client sites.
Email-only and conditional: consent and personal-data handling affect at least some of my client-site decisions.
Email-only: avoiding cookies, trackers, visitor consent, and a DPA would materially simplify my recommendations.
Not established: I currently use Google Analytics or any other analytics product.
Not established: I am presently replacing an analytics stack or have an urgent client decision.
reader_verdicts.problem_now: Privacy and consent requirements are a plausible and relevant risk when selecting client analytics, and the supplied context documents genuine developer disagreement about whether privacy-friendly analytics removes consent obligations. It is not established that I have an affected project or decision today.
reader_verdicts.stopped_at: Under GDPR, that absence of personal-data processing means a DPA is not required when using Simple Analytics.
reader_verdicts.biggest_doubt: The main benefit rests on consequential legal assertions—especially that no visitor consent or DPA is required—but the email gives no qualification, jurisdictional scope, technical explanation, or independent support. I also cannot judge whether the product has the reporting capabilities and pricing needed across client sites.
reader_verdicts.to_click_it_would_have_to: I would have clicked if this email had linked to a concise technical and legal explanation of why its collection method requires neither consent nor a DPA, while also stating the starting price and core reports included.
fixes: Rewrite “no cookies, no trackers and no visitor consent required for Simple Analytics itself” to state exactly what data is collected and link to the legal and technical basis for the consent claim.

Rewrite “Under GDPR, that absence of personal-data processing means a DPA is not required when using Simple Analytics” to qualify the scope of that conclusion and provide supporting documentation rather than presenting it as an unsupported guarantee.

Rewrite “The signup page opens a 14-day self-serve trial, so you can explore Simple Analytics on your own” to include the starting price after trial and name the core reports or capabilities I could test on a client site.
Replace “Start your 14-day trial →” with a lower-effort option such as viewing the privacy methodology, sample dashboard, pricing, and trial requirements before creating an account.

Selected audience: Agency or freelance developer choosing the analytics stack for client sites.
Research context describes some members of this market, not this recipient's installed tools or experiences. Follow the campaign request when it scopes the job.
Observed situation (inferred; check applicability): The corpus contains public developer discussion (two Hacker News threads) about whether websites need cookie consent banners and about named analytics tools (Google Analytics, Fathom, Plausible, SimpleAnalytics), but no quote in either thread identifies the speaker as an agency or freelance developer building or maintaining multiple client websites, or as selecting an analytics default on behalf of clients. The audience's defining workflow (choosing a repeatable analytics default across client builds to avoid consent-banner/DPA friction) is not directly evidenced here; only general developer debate about consent and analytics tool choice is present.
brief.reader_segment: Agency or freelance developer choosing the analytics stack for client sites
brief.promise: Simple Analytics gives developers a documented way to offer website analytics without cookies, trackers or personal-data processing, making it a concrete option when visitor consent and DPA requirements affect the stack decision.
brief.orientation: Simple Analytics is a cookie-free website analytics option for agencies and freelance developers evaluating a repeatable default across client sites, with per-site installation and documented privacy conditions.
brief.arc: In one email, move the reader from skepticism about broad privacy-friendly claims to a specific, testable proposition: Simple Analytics documents that it uses no cookies or trackers, requires no visitor consent and does not process personal data, then offers a self-guided trial as the next step.
brief.sequence_rationale: A single-email acquisition campaign needs the strongest supported reason to adopt, not a catalogue of privacy, hosting, pricing and measurement features. The consent and personal-data mechanism directly addresses the selected audience's verified uncertainty about whether privacy-friendly analytics really changes consent and DPA requirements. The email should establish that mechanism, qualify it as Simple Analytics' documented behavior rather than universal legal advice, and invite a self-guided evaluation. An assisted GA4 comparison is retained only as an alternative proposition because the recipient's use of GA4 is unknown. The single thing that would most change this campaign: Can this source be supplied in a readable form or its missing details verified?

emails.selection_reason: Consent and personal-data handling are documented decision criteria for this audience, and Simple Analytics has direct evidence for the mechanism rather than relying on the vague label “privacy-friendly.”

value_case.reader_benefit: For client sites where consent and DPA requirements shape the analytics choice, the developer can consider an analytics option designed to provide website measurement without processing personal data or requiring visitor consent for Simple Analytics itself.
value_case.mechanism: Simple Analytics uses no cookies or trackers and states that visitor consent is not required. It also states that it does not process personal data, which is why a DPA is not required under the documented GDPR basis.
decision_conditions: Apply the claim to Simple Analytics' documented data practices, not as universal legal advice for every client configuration or jurisdiction.
Each client website still requires its own appropriate installation and fit assessment.

claim_conditions: The no-consent claim concerns Simple Analytics' own documented operation.
The DPA statement is based on Simple Analytics not processing personal data and should not be generalized to every vendor, client configuration or jurisdiction.

emails.single_idea: If consent and personal-data processing affect what you can recommend to clients, Simple Analytics is worth considering because it operates without cookies or trackers, requires no visitor consent for its analytics and states that it does not process personal data.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: For a reader actively evaluating analytics alongside GA4, an assisted comparison is a distinct reason to engage: it defines a measurement question and reviews methodological causes over a fixed 30-day run.

value_case.reader_benefit: A developer or agency with an active GA4 comparison can evaluate reported pageview trends on a real site while receiving help interpreting differences instead of treating the raw gap as a consent-rejection figure.
value_case.mechanism: The assisted proof of concept begins by defining the measurement question, then runs Simple Analytics alongside GA4 for 30 days and reviews weekly trends against factors including duplicate tags, SPA routing, bot filtering, consent configuration and reporting identity.
decision_conditions: Relevant only when the reader has an active GA4 comparison to run.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: If you need to compare Simple Analytics with GA4 on a real site, the free 30-day assisted proof of concept provides a defined measurement question and a weekly review of the methodological causes behind differing pageview trends.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Define the measurement question with Simple Analytics, run both systems alongside the existing consent setup for 30 days, and review weekly pageview trends against documented methodological causes.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: a side-by-side analytics comparison is just two totals with an ambiguous gap. After: the reader sees a structured, assisted way to examine the methodological factors behind that gap on their own site.
must_not_say: Do not assume the recipient currently uses GA4; make the proposition conditional.
Do not describe the pageview gap as a consent-rejection rate or promise to isolate a consent-specific figure.

Do not present the assisted proof of concept as part of the self-serve trial.
alternative_arguments.objection: A raw comparison could produce different totals without explaining what caused the difference.
alternative_arguments.call_to_action: Book a demo to define what you would compare in the free 30-day proof of concept.
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether an assisted 30-day comparison alongside GA4 is appropriate for the site's measurement question.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The demo begins the process of discussing the GA4 setup, defining the measurement question and agreeing what the 30-day comparison should examine.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: Booking the demo does not establish the eventual size or cause of any pageview difference and does not produce a consent-rejection rate.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Signal a concrete 30-day side-by-side evaluation, while making clear that the purpose is to understand the numbers rather than promise a predetermined gap.

emails.belief_shift: Before: “privacy-friendly” is an ambiguous category claim. After: Simple Analytics has a specific operating model the reader can evaluate—no cookies, no trackers, no required visitor consent and no personal-data processing.
must_not_say: Do not claim that every client site or jurisdiction can remove its entire consent banner solely by installing Simple Analytics.
Do not claim universal legal compliance or give legal advice.

emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Simple Analytics' documented privacy model and product experience are suitable for a client-site analytics evaluation.

emails.subject_strategy: Lead with the concrete operating distinction—analytics without cookies, trackers or personal-data processing—rather than a generic privacy claim or fear-based compliance language.

brief.voice_notes: Use “we” for Simple Analytics and “you” for the reader. Keep sentences short and causal. Avoid superlatives, urgency, legalistic language and unsupported claims about competing tools.

allowed_claims: Simple Analytics requires no cookies, no trackers, and no consent from visitors.

Simple Analytics collects and stores how long a page is viewed, counting seconds only while the page is visible and not when it is hidden.

All analytics data is processed in the Netherlands (EU-hosted).
No IP addresses are stored; they are discarded immediately.
Data is encrypted, and only Simple Analytics controls the decryption keys.
Simple Analytics is hosted on infrastructure from Worldstream and Leaseweb.
